notes.meaning: The story opens when Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem. This was the first of his attacks on Judah, and it began the long exile in Babylon. Jeremiah calls it the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Commentators explain that Daniel counts from when the army set out, while Jeremiah counts from when the city was taken.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern critics hold that the book was written much later, around the time of the Maccabees (about 165 BC), rather than by Daniel himself during the exile.

notes.meaning: Babylon did not win by its own strength. The Lord handed Jehoiakim over as a judgment on his unfaithful people. Some of the holy cups and bowls from God's temple were carried to Shinar, an old name for Babylonia, and put in the temple of Babylon's god, Bel. Only part of them was taken at this time. Later these same vessels play a part in Belshazzar's downfall in chapter 5.

The king told his chief official, Ashpenaz, to pick out young men from Judah's royal and noble families. This fulfilled Isaiah's warning that some of the king's descendants would serve in Babylon's palace. The king wanted teenagers who were healthy, good-looking, bright and quick to learn. They would be taught the Babylonian language and learning. They also served as hostages, which helped keep their families back home in line.

The young men were given food and wine from the king's own table, and three years of training. This looked generous. But the king's goal was to win their loyalty and make them forget their own people. After the training they would serve in his court.

Four of the young men were from the tribe of Judah, the royal tribe. They were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. They were probably from noble or royal families. The book names only these four because its story is about them.

Each of their Hebrew names honored the true God. Daniel means "God is my Judge." Azariah means "the Lord helps." Their new names were tied to Babylon's gods, such as Bel and Nebo. Renaming them showed that they now belonged to their masters. It was also meant to slowly pull them away from the God of their fathers. Yet Scripture keeps calling Daniel by the name that points to God.

Daniel firmly made up his mind not to make himself unclean with the king's food and wine. The commentaries give several reasons. Some of the meat was forbidden by God's law. The food and wine were often first offered to idols. And rich court food could make him love Babylon and forget who he was. He did not make a scene. He politely asked permission, and his three friends joined him.

The official's kindness toward Daniel is credited to God. God moved this man's heart to treat Daniel kindly, as He had done for Joseph in Egypt. The favor we receive from others is God's gift. We should thank Him for it.

The official was afraid. If the young men looked thinner than others their age, the king might have him put to death. A ruler like Nebuchadnezzar could order that in a moment of anger. Still, he answered gently and did not report Daniel to the king.

Daniel did not give up after the first answer. He went to the steward who had daily charge of the four young men and their food. Older Bibles call him "Melzar," which is most likely the title of his job.

Daniel offered a short, safe test. For ten days they would have only vegetables and water. The word means plants grown from seed, such as grains and beans. Then the steward could compare them with the others and decide. Daniel was trusting God to bless the plain food. Calvin adds that God's Spirit guided him to suggest this plan.
The steward agreed and tested them for ten days. Ten days was long enough to see a difference in how they looked.

After ten days the four looked healthier and stronger than those eating the king's food. Plain food played some part, but the commentaries credit this mainly to God's special blessing. It shows that people do not live by bread alone, but by God's word.

So the steward kept giving them vegetables instead of the king's food and wine. Their early habit of saying no to themselves helped prepare them for later tests, like the fiery furnace and the lions' den.

They studied hard, but it was God who gave the four young men knowledge and skill. This meant real learning, not the forbidden magic of Babylon. Daniel received something more. God gave him understanding of visions and dreams, as He had given Joseph. This was the gift of a prophet, someone God speaks through.
At the end of the three years of training, the chief official brought all the young men to Nebuchadnezzar. This group included others besides these four.
The king questioned them himself. No one matched these four. So they "stood before the king," which means they were given places of honor and trust near the throne.

Whenever the king asked them about matters of wisdom, he found them ten times better than all his magicians and enchanters. Through these young captives, God humbled Babylon's pride and honored His own people.

Daniel lived past this date, since chapter 10 mentions the third year of Cyrus. But the first year of King Cyrus was when the Jews were allowed to go home. So the verse means Daniel served through the whole exile. One of the first captives lived to see his people set free.
